A component this tab also shows, such as one in a section pinned from another tab, is landed on in place. Picking a tab opens it; picking the tab you are on scrolls back to its top. In the editor, pending changes are saved before leaving the tab; if the save fails, you stay on the tab and a notification says so.

Search works in view mode, in edit mode and on public dashboards. The shortcut is ignored while you type in a field or in the code editor.

Known limit

A filter folded under a filter bar's More filters, or a map panel the reader has hidden, is not uncovered. You get a That component is not on screen notice instead.

docs.title: Unauthenticated Mode
docs.text:
Renamed to Public Mode

This page describes the legacy "Unauthenticated Mode" which has been renamed to Public Mode. The env var DEPICTIO_AUTH_UNAUTHENTICATED_MODE still works as a backward-compatible alias. See Authentication Modes for the full overview of all four modes.

docs.title: What is Unauthenticated Mode?
docs.text:
In unauthenticated mode, user lands as a temporary anonymous user with limited access. This anonymous user can only access the existing public dashboards and play with the interactive features in a stateless manner (no database persistence), but cannot create or modify dashboards. This mode is ideal for quick demonstrations or public sharing of dashboards without requiring user authentication.

If the user wants to create its own dashboard, modify existing ones using the same dataset, or create its own basic project and upload a dataset, they can switch to a temporary authenticated user mode. The temporary user will have a limited session duration (24h by default), after which dashboards will be cleared.

Example unauthenticated mode URL is available on documentation landing page: https://depictio.github.io/depictio-docs/latest/.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Unauthenticated mode landing page - AnonymousUser is logged as anonymous and needs to login to access more features (create/duplicate dashboards, create project, upload dataset)

Account status switch modalOnce the user wants to access more features, they can switch to a temporary authenticated user mode. The user and the related session information (dashboards, projects, etc.) will be stored temporarily (24h by default).

Unauthenticated mode landing page - Temporary userUser is now logged in as a temporary user and can access more features (create/duplicate dashboards, create project, upload dataset) for a limited time (24h by default).

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Enable unauthenticated mode by setting these environment variables:

# Enable unauthenticated access
DEPICTIO_AUTH_UNAUTHENTICATED_MODE=true

# Configure anonymous user settings
DEPICTIO_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_USER_EMAIL=anonymous@depict.io
DEPICTIO_AUTH_TEMPORARY_USER_EXPIRY_HOURS=24

docs.title: Helm Deployment
docs.text:
For Kubernetes deployments, use the provided values files:

# Deploy with unauthenticated mode
helm upgrade --install your-release ./helm-charts/depictio \
  -f ./helm-charts/depictio/values.yaml \
  -f ./helm-charts/depictio/values-unauth.yaml \
  -n your-namespace

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Session-Based: Data and dashboards expire after configured time
  • No Persistence: User data is not permanently stored
  • No User Management: No user accounts, groups, or permissions
  • Temporary Storage: All content is ephemeral

docs.title: Scientific Outreach and Demonstrations
docs.text:
• Public sharing of dashboards
  • Public demos and presentations

docs.title: Educational Use
docs.text:
• Training sessions
  • Workshops and tutorials
  • Proof-of-concept deployments

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Public Access: Anyone can access the deployment
  • Data Sensitivity: Only use with non-sensitive, public data (e.g., public & published datasets ; data powering the visualizations could be extracted from the dashboard by scrapping the page)
  • Resource Limits: Configure appropriate resource constraints
  • Network Security: Use proper network isolation and ingress controls

docs.title: Paper and Classic (v1.17.0+)
docs.text:
Depictio comes in two looks, with the same pages, panels and settings:

  • Paper, the default since v1.17.0: every page on paper panels, a top bar with the page or dashboard title, and a sidebar. On a dashboard, the tab sidebar folds to an icon rail, by itself while the filter panel is open, and a floating dock holds Search, Analysis, Comments and Edit / Save / Exit as icon keys. Drag it by its grip, or use the arrow keys, to the bottom, left, right or top of the page; the browser keeps the place.
  • Classic, the layout of earlier versions: a header bar of buttons and a tab sidebar.
PaperClassic

A page takes the first of:

  1. ?chrome=glass (Paper) or ?chrome=base (Classic) in its URL, kept for the rest of the browser session, for support and testing;
  2. your own pick, in Account settings → Preferences → Look, kept in this browser;
  3. the default an administrator sets in Administration → Branding → Default look;
  4. Paper.

Screenshots in these docs show one look or the other; where a control sits in the header in Classic, Paper has it in the top bar or the dock.

docs.title: Registering an Account (Sign Up)
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the Registration page by clicking the Register button on the login screen.

  1. Enter your email address in the "Email" field.

  2. Create a password and enter it in the "Password" field. You can click the eye icon to view the password as you type and Confirm your password by re-entering it in the "Confirm Password" field.

  3. Click the Register button to submit your registration details.

  4. After successful registration, you can return to the login page by clicking the Back to Login button.

docs.title: Logging In (Sign In)
docs.text:
1. Open the Depictio Login page.
  2. Enter your email address in the "Email" field.
  3. Enter your password in the "Password" field.
  4. If you want to see the password as you type it, click the eye icon next to the password field.
  5. Once both fields are filled in, click the Login button.
  6. You will be redirected to the Depictio landing page (currently /dashboards).

docs.title: Google OAuth Login
docs.text:
If you have configured Google OAuth for your Depictio instance (see Configuration), you can log in using your Google account. If the account does not exist, it will be created automatically.

When the server refuses the sign-in, for example because registration is closed, the callback page shows Sign-in failed and the reason, since v1.17.2.

docs.title: SSO login (v1.18.0+)
docs.text: An instance with SAML single sign-on adds a button, Sign in with SSO or the label it sets, that sends you to your institution's identity provider and back.

docs.title: Landing page / Dashboards section (/dashboards)
docs.text:
The listing opens on the Table view (v1.12.0+), one row per dashboard. In the Thumbnails view each dashboard is shown as a card. Cards display the dashboard's screenshot thumbnail once one has been captured, and fall back to the dashboard's logo (when set) before the generic placeholder.

The table view has a Last viewed column (v1.11.0+), sorted newest first, with dashboards you never opened last. It is kept per browser.

The Table display menu (v1.17.0+) sets the row height, Comfortable or Compact, and which columns show, with Show all and Reset. The Projects listing has the same menu. On a narrow screen the actions column stays pinned to the right edge while the table scrolls (v1.17.3+).

Dashboards are grouped into sections, each dashboard in one only, in this order: nf-core dashboards, Demo dashboards, Public, Accessed and Owned. Since v1.17.2 the nf-core section holds every dashboard of an nf-core workflow, the imported templates included: the seeded ones first, then the others by title.

docs.title: Thumbnails or table (v1.11.2+)
docs.text:
The view switcher in the toolbar picks between Thumbnails, the card grid, and Table, with sortable columns and bulk selection. The Tiles view of earlier versions is gone, and a browser that had it opens on Thumbnails.

In Thumbnails, the Card display menu beside the switcher sets:

  • Cards per row: 5 by default since v1.12.0, or 2 to 6, or Auto. Auto never makes more columns than a section has cards, so a section with a single dashboard draws it across the whole width.
  • Badges: which of Project, Template, Owner, Visibility, Last modified and Tabs a card shows. Hovering a badge gives its long form.

Reset to defaults restores both, so five cards per row. They are layout preferences, kept in the browser and left out of shared links. A browser that opened the listing before v1.12.0 stored Auto, the former default, and keeps it until you pick another value or reset. Resting the pointer on a thumbnail opens a larger, sharper preview.

Someone who never picked a view gets the one the deployment sets with DEPICTIO_VIEWER_DASHBOARDS_DEFAULT_VIEW: Table since v1.12.0, Thumbnails before. Set it to thumbnails to open the grid again. A view picked in the browser, or named by a shared link such as /dashboards?view=thumbnails, wins over it.

docs.title: Sidebar Navigation
docs.text:
The left sidebar provides easy access to various sections of the application. This includes:

  • Dashboards: View and manage your dashboards.
  • Projects: Manage your projects and data collections.
  • Administration (sysadmin users only): Access administrative features (only available to users with admin privileges).
  • About: Information about the application and its repository.

The button at the top of the sidebar folds it to icons. The top bar holds the theme toggle and your avatar, which opens Account settings (v1.17.0+). The compass in the header of the Dashboards and Projects pages starts the guided tour.

docs.title: Server information (v1.17.0+)
docs.text:
The server status at the foot of the sidebar, Online with the server version, opens the server information: version, API, mode, and links to the documentation, GitHub, the releases and the issue tracker. On a dashboard it sits at the foot of the tab rail, and in Classic it is the version badge.

For administrators, its last line says whether a newer Depictio release is out. When one is, a dot marks the status and a card in the popover names the release; OK hides it until the next one. See Release check.

docs.title: Creating a New Dashboard
docs.text:
1. On the landing page, click the orange "+ New Dashboard" button located in the top right corner.
  2. A pop-up window will appear with a field labeled "Dashboard Title".
  3. Enter a name for your new dashboard.
  4. Your dashboard will be created with the title you provided and added to the section.
  5. Click the blue "Create Dashboard" button to create the dashboard.
  6. The new dashboard will appear in the section with informations including name, owner and status (public/private).

docs.title: Viewing a Dashboard
docs.text:
1. Once a dashboard is created, it will appear under the section.
  2. Click the "View" button next to the dashboard name to open and explore its content.

docs.title: Deleting a Dashboard
docs.text:
1. To delete a dashboard, locate the dashboard in the section.
  2. Click the red "Delete" button next to the dashboard name.
  3. A confirmation pop-up will appear, asking "Are you sure you want to delete this dashboard?".
  4. Click "Delete" to permanently remove the dashboard, or "Cancel" to keep it.

docs.title: Editing dashboard name
docs.text:
1. To edit the name of a dashboard, locate the dashboard in the section.
  2. Click the "Edit name" button next to the dashboard name.
  3. A pop-up window will appear with a field labeled "New name".
  4. Enter a new name for your dashboard.
  5. Click the blue "Save" button to save the new name.

docs.title: Duplicating a dashboard
docs.text:
1. To duplicate a dashboard, locate the dashboard in the section.
  2. Click the "Duplicate" button next to the dashboard name.
  3. The dashboard will be duplicated and added to the section with the suffix "(copy)".

Note

Both "public" and "private" dashboards are listed in the Dashboards section. Public dashboards are accessible to all users, while private dashboards are only visible to the user who created them. Only the user who created a private dashboard can edit, or delete it.

docs.title: Share a filtered listing (v1.10.1+)
docs.text:
The filters of /dashboards and /projects are kept in the URL. Set them, then press the link button in the toolbar to copy a link to that view:

Link Shows /dashboards?template=nf-core/rnaseq Dashboards built from nf-core/rnaseq, any version /projects?template=nf-core/rnaseq,nf-core/viralrecon Projects built from either pipeline

Whoever opens it sees a Shared view banner, with Show everything to clear the filters. The link grants no access: it only narrows what they could already open.

docs.title: Projects section (/projects)
docs.text:
Complete Projects Documentation

For comprehensive information about Projects in Depictio, see the dedicated Projects Guide.

The Projects Guide covers:

  • Project Types - Basic vs Advanced projects
  • Creating Projects - Step-by-step instructions
  • Configuration - YAML setup and examples
  • Data Collections - File organization and processing
  • Permissions - Access control and collaboration
  • Best Practices - Optimization and troubleshooting

Quick Links:

  • Projects Guide - Complete project management
  • YAML Examples - Configuration patterns
  • Configuration Reference - Full parameter reference

docs.title: Quick Overview
docs.text:
• The left sidebar includes a "Projects" section where users can manage their projects
  • Click on "Projects" to navigate and view them
  • Projects organize your data and provide structure for dashboards
  • You can access workflows and data collections recursively within each project
  • Each entity allows you to view configuration details and preview data

docs.title: Creating a project from a run folder or a manifest (v1.16.0+)
docs.text:
+ New Project offers four tabs: Create New, Import, From Manifest and From a run folder. The last two build a project from data the server reads, with no CLI involved, in three steps: Source, Preview (a dry run, nothing is created) and Create.

  • From a run folder: point at the results folder of one pipeline run, in a bucket or, on a depictio local server, on this computer. Depictio recognises the pipeline, picks the template and shows what each data collection finds there; the data is ingested in the background. See From a run folder.
  • From Manifest: paste the URL of a data manifest and pick a template that reads one. See From a manifest.

docs.title: Account settings (/profile) (v1.17.0+)
docs.text:
Your avatar in the top bar opens Account settings, one page of sections that open and close:

  • Account: your email, role and dates. Click the avatar to upload a profile picture; the server stores it as a 256-pixel WebP and includes it in backups. Signing in with Google sets your Google picture until you upload one. Since v1.18.0 it shows your group badges (crown for P.I., shield for group admin), which open /groups, and the name and title your identity provider gives.
  • Password: change the password you sign in with.
  • CLI agents: the long-lived tokens of the depictio command line, see Create a CLI configuration. The former /cli-agents page leads here.
  • Preferences, kept in this browser: Theme, light or dark; Look, Paper, Classic or the instance default; Font size of figures, tables and cards.
  • Getting started: replay the guided tour of the app or of the builder.
  • Server: the server information.

Sign out is at the foot of the page.

AccountPreferences

docs.title: About section (/about)
docs.text: The About section provides information about the GitHub repository and the documentation.

docs.title: Admin section (/admin)
docs.text:
The Admin section is only accessible to users with admin privileges. Since v1.17.0 its pages are listed down the side, in four groups:

Group Pages People Users: every account, its role (standard or system admin), deletion and, since v1.19.0, Add user. Groups (v1.18.0+): see Groups Content Projects and Dashboards: every one of them, whoever owns it. Admins can delete any Activity Tasks, Ingestion, Watchers, Logs and Health, see Monitoring Instance Branding, Backups, Maintenance and Settings

docs.title: Adding a user (v1.19.0+)
docs.text:
Administration → Users → Add user creates an account with an email, a display name and an initial password, generated by default (with refresh and copy). Two switches: ask for a new password at first sign-in, on by default, and system admin. A person asked to change it is taken to the Password section of Account settings until they do, and the Users list shows the pending change.

It works even when registration or password sign-in is closed: on an SSO-only instance the account is matched by email at the first SSO sign-in, which is how a person is added to a group before they ever sign in. It is not offered in single-user or public mode.

docs.title: Release check (v1.17.0+)
docs.text:
Administration → Settings → Version check tells administrators when a newer Depictio release is published. The server asks the GitHub Releases API of depictio/depictio every 6 hours, with a plain request that sends nothing about the instance, and the server information shows the result to administrators only. Check now asks at once.

The check is on by default and the switch turns it off for the instance. Setting DEPICTIO_VERSION_CHECK_ENABLED to true or false decides instead and locks the switch, for instances that must make no outbound call.

Since v1.18.0 the check also runs as soon as the running version is not the one that last checked, so the page never shows a latest release older than the current one after an upgrade.

docs.title: Page reference
docs.text: Depictio's main pages and their URLs:

docs.title: Project detail (/projects/{id})
docs.text:
A single project's data. Since v1.17.0 the page starts with the project's type and its workflows, as cards to pick one from, then a switch between two views:

  • Data collections — the project's workflows, a sortable, filterable table of its data collections, its cross-DC links, and the details of the selected collection. For a composed project, a Files the catalog did not recognise card lists the tables left out, with the command that adds each (v1.16.0+).
  • Ingestion — the ingestion report, offered for every project since v1.6.0. For one created from a pipeline template it compares expected against ingested data collections; for any other it reads the collections the project declares today, and a Live project badge says so. Since v1.15.0 a History view lists the project's ingestion runs, and, where the server allows it, Run ingestion starts one from the browser.

Selecting a data collection shows its details, including its Delta version, and for a table a data preview and its Version history: see Dataset history.

You can reach this page directly by clicking the project badge shown on any dashboard card or in the dashboards table, or the project name in an open dashboard's Settings (v1.6.0+).

Data that is not on the server's own disk is handled in two places (v1.16.0+); the mechanisms are described on Remote data and manifests.

  • Remote URL in Create Data Collection: the Table (CSV / TSV / Parquet) tab offers Upload a file or Remote URL. With the latter, paste an https:// or s3:// address as the File URL (http:// only when the server allows it); the name and format are filled in from its last segment. The server fetches the file, so it never travels through the browser, and a private bucket is read with the project's storage settings. MultiQC reports are uploaded only.
  • Project settings in the header, next to Permissions, opens three sections; nothing is saved on close, each acts on its own button:
    • Storage, for project owners and administrators: the endpoint, bucket, region and keys of a private bucket the project reads, with Test connection. See Project storage settings.
    • Data refresh: re-read the collections that come from a manifest, a URL or a bucket, and rebuild their tables. See Refreshing the data.
    • Export: package the project and its dashboards as a template bundle (zip). See Export a project as a template.

Data refresh and Export are for owners, editors and administrators; on a public instance, administrators only. The dialog opens on the section used last.

docs.title: Dashboard viewer (/dashboard/{id})
docs.text: Read-only dashboard with filters and component interactions.

docs.title: Dashboard editor (/dashboard-edit/{id})
docs.text: Design mode — add, configure, and arrange components.

docs.title: CLI agents / tokens (/profile#cli-agents)
docs.text: Generate and manage CLI configurations for the depictio CLI. Saved as ~/.depictio/CLI.yaml, a configuration is the server every CLI command uses by default. Since v1.17.0 they are a section of Account settings, and /cli-agents leads there.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
Everything you need to configure and manage Depictio projects.

Page Description Guide Project types (Basic, Advanced, Template) and lifecycle YAML Examples Configuration patterns with annotated examples Full Reference Complete YAML field reference Recipes Data transformation recipes for bioinformatics pipelines Templates One-command project setup for nf-core pipelines Composed dashboards (v1.16.0+) A dashboard built from what the tools catalog recognises in a results directory no template fits Remote data and manifests (v1.16.0+) Ingest a run folder on S3, bind a data collection to a URL or an S3 prefix, or read a data manifest; create projects from the web UI, refresh and share them

docs.title: Composed dashboards (v1.16.0+)
docs.text:
When no bundled template fits a results directory, depictio ingest builds the dashboard from what it finds there, the way MultiQC builds its report: each file the tools catalog recognises becomes a data collection with the tiles the catalog gives it, laid out in one tab per pipeline stage. The result is an ordinary template, so ingestion, refreshes and the dashboard import work as they do with a bundled one.

# No bundled template fits: the dashboard is composed from the catalog
depictio ingest results/

# Compose even when a bundled template fits, and add the files the catalog does not know
depictio ingest results/ --compose --include-unknown

# Look first, offline: print what would be composed and write an editable template
depictio template compose results/ -o my_template/
depictio ingest results/ --template my_template/

Here a results directory no bundled template fits is previewed with depictio template compose, then ingested into the local server, which composes the same template and imports the dashboard:

docs.title: When a dashboard is composed
docs.text:
depictio ingest takes its project from the first of these that applies (see Which template a run uses):

  1. --template or --project-config-path;
  2. --pipeline-id;
  3. a bundled template detected from the run's own records, such as an nf-core run's pipeline_info/;
  4. a template composed from the catalog.

--compose skips the third: it composes even when a bundled template fits. It cannot be combined with --template or --project-config-path.

Only a local DATA_DIR is composed, since the catalog is matched against a walk of the directory:

  • An s3:// run folder, --manifest or --bind without DATA_DIR still need a template. The web UI's From a run folder does not compose either: a folder no template reads gets No matching template, and a pipeline has to be picked.
  • The Nextflow trigger passes --pipeline-id for every pipeline that declares a manifest, so a pipeline Depictio ships no template for stops at the second step, with exit code 1, rather than being composed. Run depictio ingest <results dir> yourself.

When the catalog recognises nothing in the directory, the run stops with exit code 1: Nothing in … is recognised by the catalog. The message says how many tabular files the directory holds, which --include-unknown would ingest.

docs.title: What is recognised
docs.text:
• The directory is walked once, hidden folders and a top-level work/ folder left out, and each catalog output's find (a file name or a path glob) is matched against that walk.
  • Every multiqc.parquet becomes a MultiQC collection, wherever it sits. Its plots are listed off the report itself, so the multiqc package is not needed to compose.
  • An output the catalog reads as it is becomes a table collection of the files found, in CSV, TSV or parquet.
  • An output that a recipe reshapes becomes a recipe collection whose sources point at the files found. A file is kept for a recipe only when it has the input columns the recipe declares, so a broad find such as *.tsv does not take another tool's tables. A recipe that parses whole reports (Picard, RSeQC, samtools stats, Bowtie 2 logs) gets them one line per row, as the bundled templates scan them, and a collection that a recipe reads is created for it from the raw files when the run has none.
  • Each output's renders become tiles, kept when the collection has the columns they bind and the dashboard models accept them.
  • Every composed collection is optional: one that fails to ingest is skipped and the import drops its tiles, instead of the run failing.

Before ingesting, the CLI prints what it decided:

  • Recognised: each collection with its tool, its stage and its files;
  • the tabs, the key metrics, and whether general statistics were joined;
  • Left out, with a reason for each: a file the scan cannot read, a render whose columns are missing, a recipe whose input is absent, a table written twice as .csv and .tsv;
  • Not recognised: the tabular files the catalog does not know, with what each could show. The count in its heading also takes in the files that could not be read as a table, which get no line.

depictio ingest shows the first 15 items left out and the first 10 files not recognised; depictio template compose --verbose lists them all.

docs.title: The dashboard
docs.text:
One multi-tab dashboard:

Tab What it holds Overview About this run: the tools recognised, the MultiQC report and the tabs in pipeline order, then, when the catalog does not know some tabular files, how many were left out, with a pointer to the project page and --include-unknown (once all are added, that they are in their tool's tab or in Other data). Key metrics: the number of samples, then the cards the catalog marks as a tool's headline, eight cards in all at most. General statistics: MultiQC's General Statistics table, and Headline metrics per sample, across tools, one row per sample and one column per headline card One tab per stage Each stage present, in this order: Quality control, Alignment & coverage, Quantification, Peaks, Variants, Fusions, Taxonomy & diversity, Functional annotation, Immune repertoire, Differential analysis, Benchmarking, Other results. The subtitle lists the tools, and each tool has a section: its cards (eight at most, none twice), figures and advanced visualizations. The tables are folded under Tables, and the catalog's filters sit in a … filters section MultiQC Every plot of the report, in sections by stage. A run with several reports gets one tab each, named by what tells them apart, such as MultiQC (test_aws) Other data Only when files the catalog does not know are added The Overview of the dashboard composed in the recording above, from Depictio's catalog conformance outputs and one table the catalog does not know. The key metrics are the sample count and the headline card of mosdepth.

A tool's stage comes from the catalog. A MultiQC plot goes to the stage of the catalog's section for its module, Quality control when the catalog has none.

Colours and icons follow what a tile shows, after the bundled reference dashboards: a card's colour and icon say what it measures (the sample count is teal with a flask on every tab), no colour appears twice in a section, and a section's icon comes from its content. An nf-core run gets the nf-core icon.

Composed from nf-core/taxprofiler test results: the Taxonomy & diversity tab, with a section per tool and the Samples filter that applies to every tab.

docs.title: The Samples filter
docs.text:
The filter panel opens on one Sample filter, in a Samples section pinned at the top and marked Applies to every tab, a section on every tab. It narrows every tab:

  • samples.tsv, written next to the composed template, lists every sample of the run: the values of each collection's sample column (sample, sample_id, sampleid, sample_name or samplename), the values read off file paths, and the rows of MultiQC's General Statistics.
  • A name that extends another at a separator is the same sample: MOCK_001_Illumina_Hiseq_3000_1 in the MultiQC report is MOCK_001 when a path names MOCK_001, while S1 and S10 stay two samples. Suffixes such as .sorted.bam are removed first.
  • The filter is linked to MultiQC and to every collection that names samples: with the direct resolver when the collection uses the same names, with sample_mapping and the variants otherwise.
  • The sample filters the catalog offers per collection are dropped. A group of unrecognised files keeps its filters on columns with 2 to 12 values.

With fewer than two samples, or more than 5,000 names, no samples.tsv is written. The filter then reads the MultiQC report's own sample list; without a report, a stage tab that has no filter gets a sample filter on its first collection with a sample column.

docs.title: Files the catalog does not recognise
docs.text:
Tabular files (.csv, .tsv, .tab, .txt, .parquet) that no recognised output uses are proposed, never added silently. Files under pipeline_info/ and in the data folder of a MultiQC report are not proposed.

  • Files of one shape (the same depth, extension and columns) that differ by one value are one proposal, written as a glob: arg/abricate/*/*.txt, 19 files. The part that varies becomes a column: sample when the files have no sample column and its values turn up elsewhere in the run under other names, file otherwise, as for variants of one output such as salmon.merged.gene_*.tsv.
  • A file whose first row is data, not column names (a Kraken report), is read without a header, its columns numbered.
  • A table written twice, as .csv and as .tsv, is proposed once.
  • Each proposal says what the file would show: up to four numeric columns as cards (card: mean of reads), up to two filters on columns with 2 to 12 values, a scatter of the first two numeric columns or a box plot of one by a category, and the table.

At most 50 proposals are listed, and at most 2,000 files are read to find their shape.

docs.title: Adding them
docs.text:
--include-unknown adds every proposal. --include GLOB adds those with a file matching the glob, relative to the results directory; it is repeatable. A glob with no / matches a file name at any depth ('*.tsv'), a trailing ** takes every file below ('amp/**'), and a proposal's own glob is taken as it is. A proposal named by --include is added even past the 50 listed.

depictio ingest results/ --include 'arg/abricate/*/*.txt' --include '*_summary.tsv'

Both apply only when the dashboard is composed: with a bundled template that fits, add --compose.

An added group goes where the tool that wrote it is. When a directory on its path names a catalog tool or MultiQC module (its id, its name, or exactly one word of it, so deseq2_qc is DESeq2's), the group gets a section named after that tool, in that tool's stage tab, the deepest such directory winning. Other groups go to the Other data tab, one section per directory below what they share; a top directory that only holds tool directories, such as arg/, is looked through. At ingestion, the value a group's files differ by is added to their rows as the sample or file column, from the wildcard of its scan.

Composed from nf-core/funcscan test results with --include-unknown: the Other data tab. Abricate's 19 per-sample tables are one collection, its sample read off the path.

docs.title: On the project page
docs.text:
The Data collections tab of a composed project lists what was left out in a Files the catalog did not recognise card, below its data collections:

Column Content File The proposal's name and its path or glob, N files for a group, and the column holding the samples Columns How many, and the format; their names on hover Would show The tiles it would get

The copy button of a line copies the command that adds it, and the one in the card's header the command that adds them all:

depictio ingest '/data/run42/results' --compose --reset-dashboards --include 'arg/abricate/*/*.txt'
depictio ingest '/data/run42/results' --compose --reset-dashboards --include-unknown

The files are on the machine that ran the ingestion, which the server may not see, so the page gives a command rather than a button: run it there, against the same server. --reset-dashboards rebuilds the dashboard from the new composition, since a refresh keeps the tabs a dashboard already has as they are; edits made in the viewer are lost. Add --project when the project was given a name of its own.

docs.title: Composing offline
docs.text:
depictio template compose composes without ingesting and without a server: it prints the same report as ingest, then writes the template.

depictio template compose results/ -o my_template/
# edit my_template/template.yaml or my_template/dashboards/composed.yaml, then
depictio ingest results/ --template my_template/
File Content template.yaml The template: its id, composed/<directory>, a DATA_ROOT variable, one workflow named after the pipeline (or results) with one data collection per recognised output, the links of the Samples filter, and the files left out with their proposals dashboards/composed.yaml The dashboard general_stats.tsv The headline metrics per sample, across tools samples.tsv Every sample of the run

general_stats.tsv and samples.tsv are computed from this run and read from the template's folder: keep the folder where it is, and compose again for another run. The options are in the CLI reference.

Without -o, the template goes where depictio ingest keeps the templates it composes: ~/.depictio/composed/<directory>-<hash>/, one folder per results directory, or the same below DEPICTIO_COMPOSE_HOME when it is set. The composition is deterministic, so composing the same directory again writes the same template, and a refresh does not reshuffle the dashboard.

The project is named <directory> (<parent directory>), such as results (run42), unless --project names it.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Only a local results directory is composed: not an s3:// one, not from the web UI, and not through the Nextflow trigger for a pipeline with a manifest. See When a dashboard is composed.
  • The Samples filter reaches a collection only through a sample-named column or its file paths. A table that names samples in a column called otherwise is not linked.
  • A recipe that reads other collections is left out of the general statistics, which are computed from the files before anything is ingested.
  • Most catalog outputs render advanced visualizations, and few MultiQC modules have a catalog section of their own: their plots are all on the MultiQC tab, under Quality control.
  • An unrecognised file is added with the command from the project page, not from the browser.

  • Contributing a tool: stage, headline and priority in the catalog

docs.title: Projects in Depictio
docs.text:
Projects are the foundation of data organization in Depictio. They serve as containers for your data and dashboards, providing structure and access control for your analysis.

🎬 Projects Management Overview: Discover how Depictio's project types organize your data workflow

docs.title: Understanding Project Architecture
docs.text:
Every Depictio project contains:

  • Core Project Information - Name, description, and metadata
  • Data Organization - Either direct data collections (Basic) or workflow-based structure (Advanced)
  • Permission System - Role-based access control with owners, editors, and viewers
  • Dashboard Integration - Each dashboard is linked to a project, allowing for interactive data exploration
  • Storage Backend - Automatic conversion to Delta Lake format for optimal performance

docs.title: Basic Projects
docs.text:
Perfect for: Direct data analysis and quick insights

Use when: You have tabular data files ready for analysis and want immediate visualization capabilities.

Basic projects provide an easy onboarding experience - upload your data and start creating interactive dashboards within minutes.

🎬 Basic Project Creation: Watch how to create a basic project from scratch - upload data and start visualizing in minutes

docs.title: Core Features
docs.text:
• 🚀 Immediate Setup - No configuration files needed
  • 📁 Direct File Upload from WebUI - Drag and drop your data files
  • 🔄 Flexible Data Formats - CSV, Excel, Parquet, Feather
  • ⚡ Fast Processing - Direct conversion to Delta Lake format
  • Instant Visualization - Start creating dashboards immediately

docs.title: Supported File Formats
docs.text: Format Extension Best Use Case CSV .csv Most common, universal compatibility TSV .tsv Tab-separated, good for scientific data Excel .xlsx, .xls Business data, multiple sheets Parquet .parquet Large datasets, optimal performance Feather .feather Fast I/O, preserves data types

docs.title: Creating a Basic Project
docs.text:
Web InterfaceCLI Method
  1. Navigate to Projects - Click "Projects" in the main navigation
  2. Create Project - Click the "Create Project" button
  3. Choose Basic Type - Select "Basic Project" from the options
  4. Project Details - Fill in name and description
  5. Project data management - Navigate to the "Data Collections" tab
  6. Upload Data - Add your data files to collections by creating a new collection
    • Click "Add Data Collection"
    • Drag and drop files or use the file picker
    • Supported formats: CSV, TSV, Excel, Parquet, Feather
  7. Start Visualizing - Create dashboards with your data
  1. Create Configuration File - Write a YAML file defining your project
# Create a basic project configuration file - basic_project.yaml
name: "My Basic Project"
project_type: "basic"
data_collections:
  - data_collection_tag: "my_data"
    config:
      type: "Table"
      metatype: "Metadata"
      scan:
        mode: "single"
        scan_parameters:
          filename: "/path/to/data.csv"
      dc_specific_properties:
        format: "CSV"
        polars_kwargs:
          separator: ","
          has_header: true
  1. Run CLI Command - Use the Depictio CLI to create the project
# Process the project
depictio ingest --project-config-path basic_project.yaml

docs.title: Advanced Projects
docs.text:
Perfect for: Bioinformatics workflows and complex data pipelines

Use when: You have automated pipelines generating data with standardized file organization and need to process multiple samples systematically.

Advanced projects are designed for core facility-like setups where standardized workflows generate structured data across multiple samples, timepoints, or experimental conditions.

docs.title: Core Features
docs.text:
• 🔬 Workflow Integration - Connect to nf-core, Nextflow, Snakemake, Galaxy pipelines
  • 📊 Multi-sample Analysis - Handle large number of samples
  • 🔍 File Discovery - Regex-based pattern matching for file organization
  • 🔗 Cross-DC Links - Interactive filtering across data collections (tables, MultiQC, etc.)
  • 📈 Scalable Processing - Delta Lake backend for large-scale data

docs.title: Project Structure Example
docs.text:
study_directory/
├── depictio_project.yaml    # Configuration file
├── run_001/                 # First sample batch
│   ├── sample_A/
│   │   ├── stats/
│   │   │   └── sample_A_stats.tsv
│   │   └── analysis_results/
│   │       └── sample_A_analysis.tsv
│   └── sample_B/
│       ├── stats/
│       │   └── sample_B_stats.tsv
│       └── analysis_results/
│           └── sample_B_analysis.tsv
└── run_002/                 # Second sample batch
    ├── sample_C/
    │   ├── stats/
    │   │   └── sample_C_stats.tsv
    │   └── analysis_results/
    │       └── sample_C_analysis.tsv
    └── sample_D/
        ├── stats/
        │   └── sample_D_stats.tsv
        └── analysis_results/
            └── sample_D_analysis.tsv

docs.title: Configuration File Format
docs.text:
Advanced projects require a YAML configuration that describes data organization patterns:

# =============================================================================
# DEPICTIO ADVANCED PROJECT CONFIGURATION
# =============================================================================

# Project identification
name: "RNA-seq Expression Study"
project_type: "advanced"
description: "Multi-sample RNA sequencing analysis"
is_public: false

# Workflow definition
workflows:
  - name: "rnaseq_pipeline"

    # Workflow engine information
    engine:
      name: "nextflow" # or "snakemake", "python"
      version: "24.10.3"

    description: "nf-core RNA-seq analysis pipeline"
    repository_url: "https://github.com/my-org/my-nf-wf-rnaseq"

    # Data organization configuration
    config:
      # Data location settings
      parent_runs_location:
        - "{DATA_LOCATION}/rnaseq-results" # Environment variable
        - "/absolute/path/to/data" # Alternative absolute path

      # Run identification pattern
      runs_regex: ".*" # Matches all directories

      # Data collections definition
      data_collections:
        # Sample statistics collection
        - data_collection_tag: "sample_stats"
          description: "Per-sample quality control statistics"

          config:
            type: "Table"
            metatype: "Aggregate" # Combine multiple files

            # File discovery settings
            scan:
              mode: "recursive"
              scan_parameters:
                regex_config:
                  pattern: "stats/.*_stats.tsv"

            # Processing configuration
            dc_specific_properties:
              format: "TSV"
              polars_kwargs:
                separator: "\t"
                has_header: true

              # Column selection for performance
              keep_columns:
                - "sample_id"
                - "total_reads"
                - "mapped_reads"
                - "quality_score"

              # Human-readable descriptions
              columns_description:
                sample_id: "Unique sample identifier"
                total_reads: "Total sequencing reads"
                mapped_reads: "Successfully aligned reads"
                quality_score: "Overall sample quality metric"

        # Analysis results collection
        - data_collection_tag: "gene_expression"
          description: "Gene expression analysis results"

          config:
            type: "Table"
            metatype: "Aggregate"

            scan:
              mode: "recursive"
              scan_parameters:
                regex_config:
                  pattern: "analysis_results/.*_analysis.tsv"

            dc_specific_properties:
              format: "TSV"
              polars_kwargs:
                separator: "\t"
                has_header: true

              keep_columns:
                - "sample_id"
                - "gene_id"
                - "expression_level"
                - "p_value"

# Cross-DC Links: Interactive filtering between data collections
links:
  - source_dc_id: "sample_stats"      # Filter from this DC
    source_column: "sample_id"         # Filter by this column
    target_dc_id: "gene_expression"    # Update this DC
    target_type: "table"               # Target type: table or multiqc
    link_config:
      resolver: "direct"               # Same value in both DCs

docs.title: File Discovery Patterns
docs.text: Advanced projects use five scanning modes. Two walk a local directory tree, single and recursive. Three fetch data from where it already is, url, s3_prefix and manifest, and are covered on Remote data and manifests.

docs.title: Single File Mode
docs.text:
Perfect for metadata files or summary statistics generated once per project:

scan:
  mode: "single"
  scan_parameters:
    filename: "general_metadata_project_info.csv"

docs.title: Recursive Mode
docs.text:
Uses regex patterns to find files at any directory depth:

scan:
  mode: "recursive"
  scan_parameters:
    regex_config:
      pattern: "star_salmon/.*/quant.sf"

docs.title: Remote Modes (v1.16.0+)
docs.text:
A collection can also point at one file on the web or in a bucket (url), at every object under an S3 prefix (s3_prefix), or at the entries of a Data Manifest (manifest). Whoever ingests reads the files from there, the CLI or the server, so these modes also work from the web UI with no CLI installed, and the server can refresh them later. On the CLI, --bind TAG=LOCATION picks the mode from the shape of the location, so a template written for a local tree can be run against a bucket:

depictio ingest --template my-lab/rnaseq-qc/1 \
  --bind samples=s3://my-bucket/run42/*.samples.csv

See Remote data and manifests for the modes, the manifest contract, and how to refresh or share such a project.

docs.title: CLI Workflow
docs.text:
Process advanced projects using the CLI:

# Complete workflow execution
depictio ingest --project-config-path ./rnaseq_project.yaml

The CLI executes this pipeline:

  1. ✅ Server Check - Verify connection to Depictio backend
  2. ✅ S3 Storage Check - Validate cloud storage configuration
  3. ✅ Config Validation - Ensure YAML structure is correct
  4. ✅ Config Sync - Register project with server
  5. ✅ File Scan - Discover files matching patterns
  6. ✅ Data Process - Convert files to Delta Lake format
  7. ✅ Joins - Run the table joins the project configuration defines
  8. ✅ Dashboards - Import the dashboards the project lacks, from the template or from --dashboard

--skip STEP leaves steps out, for instance --skip dashboards. See Skipping steps.

docs.title: Managing Data Collections from the viewer (v0.12.0+)
docs.text:
Data Collections can be created and managed directly from the viewer — no YAML edits or CLI runs required. Since v1.18.0 every project offers Create Data Collection on its page, a project made by the CLI included: what you may do depends on your role, not on the project type. A later CLI refresh keeps what was added in the browser (see Refreshing a project).

Available from v0.12.0

All flows in this section require Depictio v0.12.0 or later. See the changelog for the full release notes.

docs.title: MultiQC Data Collections
docs.text:
MultiQC DCs support a full lifecycle from the Manage Data Collection modal:

Action What it does Create Upload one or more MultiQC reports (single file or folder) — the DC is materialised with cache prewarmed via Celery Append Add more runs to an existing DC; the live cache is invalidated and rewarmed Replace Swap the underlying report set in place Clear Drop all data from the DC while keeping the definition Manage Data Collection modal — the Modify data tab handles append / replace; Clear contents drops data while keeping the DC definition. Shown against a Table DC; the same shell drives the MultiQC lifecycle, with the inner upload UI swapped for multiqc-folder ingest.

docs.title: Uniformity validation (React Beta)
docs.text:
Web interface

The uniformity checklist UI and the Check now button are available in the web interface. The validator endpoint can be called from any client.

Before ingest, MultiQC reports are checked for uniformity — the same module set and column schema across runs — so plot rendering stays consistent. The check runs automatically on Create and on every Append, and can be re-run on demand with the Check now button.

Non-uniform reports surface a checklist of differences (missing modules, divergent columns) and block the destructive action until resolved.

Uniformity checks panel inside the MultiQC create flow — module set, plot keys, MultiQC version, and sample uniqueness are validated; Check now re-runs the check on demand.

docs.title: Type-specific Data Collection configuration
docs.text:
Web interface

The UI for type-specific DC configuration is available in the web interface. YAML-level configuration is supported everywhere.

Some visualization types need extra metadata declared at the Data Collection level (e.g. which columns hold coordinates, which hold sample IDs, log-fold-change, p-values, …). Declaring this on the DC means every figure built on top inherits the config — no need to re-specify it per component.

This pattern is being rolled out incrementally. The first shipped example is Map; advanced-viz types (volcano, ComplexHeatmap, UpSet, GSEA enrichment, rarefaction, …) will follow the same pattern.

docs.title: Example: Map-capable Table DCs
docs.text:
Tabular DCs can be marked Map-capable so every Map figure built on them inherits the same coordinates without re-specifying lat_column / lon_column:

  • In the React viewer: the Create DC modal has a Coordinates tab. Columns are scanned and lat/lon candidates are detected inline — you confirm or override the pick.
  • At upload time: POST /create_from_upload accepts latColumn and lonColumn query params with column-existence validation.
  • In YAML: use DCTableCoordinatesConfig on the DC's config block (see YAML examples).

Per-figure lat_column/lon_column overrides still work when set; if both are unset, the DC-level config is used.

Create Data Collection modal — Table tab. After dropping a TSV with lat/lon columns the modal surfaces a "Looks like a coordinates table" banner with column pickers and a save-as-coordinates toggle.

docs.title: Example: Phylogeny DCs and their metadata table
docs.text:
A phylogeny DC is file-backed: the .nwk / .nex file is read where it was found, never parsed or converted. What it declares at the DC level is where its tip annotations come from: a separate Table DC keyed by taxon name, the same split Microreact uses. Every phylogenetic figure built on the tree inherits that join.

- data_collection_tag: "bacterial_tree"
  description: "Bacterial phylogeny (21 taxa), Newick format"
  config:
    type: "phylogeny"
    metatype: "Aggregate"
    scan:
      mode: "single"
      scan_parameters:
        filename: "{DATA_ROOT}/trees/bacterial_tree.nwk"
    dc_specific_properties:
      format: "newick"          # or "nexus"
      ladderize: true
      metadata_dc_tag: "bacterial_metadata"
      metadata_taxon_column: "taxon"

- data_collection_tag: "bacterial_metadata"
  description: "Tip metadata (group / habitat / resistance)"
  config:
    type: "Table"
    metatype: "Aggregate"
    scan:
      mode: "single"
      scan_parameters:
        filename: "{DATA_ROOT}/trees/bacterial_metadata.tsv"
    dc_specific_properties:
      format: "TSV"
      polars_kwargs:
        separator: "\t"

Leave the three metadata keys out and the tree still renders, just unannotated. Use tip_label_strategy: "first_token" when leaf names carry a suffix (Escherichia_coli_K12 → Escherichia_coli).

A component then points at the tree with tree_wf_id / tree_dc_id and colours its tips from any column of the metadata DC. See Phylogenetic for the component schema and its controls.

docs.title: Example: Indexed-file DCs
docs.text:
An indexed_file DC is file-backed too, and it is the one to reach for when a genomic file is too large or too dense to become a table: a per-sample VCF, a BAM, a coverage bigWig, an annotation GFF3, or any bgzip-compressed, tabix-indexed interval file such as a BED. Ingestion builds no Delta table. It copies each matched file and its index sidecar to S3, one object per sample, and a genome track in the browser asks the API for presigned URLs and range-reads only the part of the file covering the region in view.

- data_collection_tag: "variant_files"
  description: "Annotated VCF per sample with its tabix index"
  optional: true
  config:
    type: "indexed_file"
    metatype: "Metadata"
    scan:
      mode: "recursive"
      scan_parameters:
        regex_config:
          pattern: ".*\\.ann\\.vcf\\.gz$"
    dc_specific_properties:
      format: "vcf"            # vcf, bam, bigwig, bigbed, gff3, fasta or tabix
      assembly: "{GENOME}"     # genome axis of the tracks reading this DC
      sample_regex: "(?P<sample>[^/]+?)\\.ann\\.vcf\\.gz$"
      max_file_size_mb: 64     # files above the cap are skipped with a warning
Key Default Meaning format required Which lazy reader the track uses. tabix covers any bgzip + tabix interval file that is not a VCF or GFF3. bw, bb and gff are accepted as aliases. index_suffix per format Suffix of the index beside each file: .tbi for vcf, gff3 and tabix, .bai for bam, .fai for fasta, none for the self-indexed bigwig and bigbed. Set it only when the pipeline names its indexes differently; an empty string declares a self-indexed file. sample_regex file name A regular expression with a named sample group, matched against the file path. Without it, the file name minus its format and compression suffixes is the sample. sample_col sample The name the sample id has in the project's tables, so a file track can sit beside table-backed tracks and answer the dashboard's sample filter. It is not a column of this DC. assembly none Genome assembly the files are aligned to. Left out, the component config decides. max_file_size_mb 512 Per-file upload cap.

The scan matches one primary file per sample. A file with no index beside it is skipped with a warning rather than uploaded unreadable, and a second file resolving to a sample already taken is skipped too, so which file wins never depends on scan order. Making the DC optional, as above, keeps a run that was fetched without its index sidecars from failing the whole ingestion.

Prefer a table DC when the data is small enough to filter and aggregate as rows: cards, figures and tables read rows, and an indexed_file DC has none. Its consumer is a genome track reading files directly: a Genome view tile with source: file.

docs.title: Storage the browser can read (v1.13.0+)
docs.text:
The bytes of an indexed file never pass through the API: the browser reads them from the object store itself, with the presigned URLs the API hands out (valid 15 minutes). Two things follow for a deployment:

  • The URLs are signed for the address the browser uses. The API signs them against DEPICTIO_S3_PUBLIC_URL when it is set, otherwise against DEPICTIO_S3_EXTERNAL_PROTOCOL, DEPICTIO_S3_EXTERNAL_HOST and DEPICTIO_S3_EXTERNAL_PORT (the older DEPICTIO_MINIO_* names still work). A signature covers the host, so a URL signed for an in-cluster name such as http://s3:9000 fails in the browser.
  • The store must answer the viewer's origin with CORS and serve range requests. The bundled SeaweedFS allows every origin by default; narrow it with -s3.allowedOrigins=https://viewer.example.org, through the s3 service's command in Docker Compose or s3.extraArgs in the Helm chart. On AWS S3 or another gateway, add a bucket CORS rule allowing GET and HEAD from the viewer's origin, with Range among the allowed headers and Content-Range, Content-Length, Accept-Ranges and ETag exposed.

Without this, a genome view shows no file tracks. Tracks read from table DCs are unaffected.

docs.title: Example: genomic_tracks DCs
docs.text:
A genomic_tracks DC is a manifest of track files: one row per bigWig, narrowPeak, BAM, VCF or other genome-browser file, with the file's location in uri_column. The manifest is ingested like a table, so it can be filtered, linked and joined like one, and the genome browser shows the tracks of the rows left after filtering. The track files themselves stay files: a relative uri is uploaded to Depictio's S3 at ingestion, and an s3:// or https:// one is read in place.

This is the DC of the nf-core/chipseq dashboard template:

- data_collection_tag: "tracks"
  description: "Genome-browser tracks of the run, one row per file"
  config:
    type: "genomic_tracks"
    metatype: "Metadata"
    source: "transformed"
    transform:
      recipe: "nf-core/chipseq/tracks.py"   # builds the manifest from the run's results
    dc_specific_properties:
      format: "TSV"
      uri_column: "uri"
      track_id_column: "track_id"
      sample_column: "sample_id"            # what a link or a click filters on
      format_column: "format"
      name_column: "name"
      color_column: "color"
      category_column: "category"
      order_column: "order"
      assembly: "hg19"
      display_defaults:                     # JBrowse config merged into every track of a format
        bigwig:
          displays:
            - type: "LinearWiggleDisplay"
              height: 60
              autoscale: "local"

A project that writes its own manifest uses scan instead of transform, pointing at the TSV, and can set remote_base_uri to read relative uri values in place under an s3:// or https:// prefix instead of uploading them. Only hosts and buckets on the server's allow-list can be read in place, see Security.

Key Default Meaning uri_column uri Column holding the track location: a relative path, an s3:// URI or an https:// URL. track_id_column the uri Column with a unique id per track. sample_column none The entity a track belongs to (sample, cell, ...). Cross-filtering and the browser's selection use it. format_column format Column with the track format. Without it the format is read from the file extension, falling back to default_format. index_column index_uri Column with the index location. Left empty, the conventional sibling is used (.bai, .crai, .tbi, .fai). name_column, color_column, category_column, order_column none Track label, colour, folder in the track selector, and the order the tracks open in. assembly hg38 A preset (hg38, hg19, hs1, mm10, mm39, sacCer3, dm6, ce11, danRer11, TAIR10, wuhCor1) or a custom assembly given by a FASTA with its index, or a 2bit file. direct_access false Let the browser fetch https:// tracks itself instead of through the API. The host must send CORS and Range headers.

Supported formats are bigWig, bedGraph, BED, bigBed, narrowPeak, broadPeak, VCF, BAM, CRAM, GFF3, GTF and FASTA. A link whose target_type is genomic_tracks lets a table selection pick the tracks to show, and a click in the browser filters the other components back, see Cross-DC filtering.

For per-sample files read directly by a Genome view tile, with no manifest, see Indexed-file DCs.

docs.title: Example: Protein structure DCs (v1.19.0+)
docs.text:
Protein structures and predicted aligned error (PAE) matrices are indexed_file DCs too, one file per protein. They need no index: a protein tile fetches the file whole.

- data_collection_tag: "structures"
  description: "Top-ranked predicted structure per target"
  config:
    type: "indexed_file"
    metatype: "Metadata"
    scan:
      mode: "recursive"
      scan_parameters:
        regex_config:
          pattern: ".*/top_ranked_structures/[^/]+\\.pdb$"
    dc_specific_properties:
      format: "pdb"            # pdb, mmcif or pae
      sample_regex: "top_ranked_structures/(?P<sample>[^/]+?)\\.pdb$"
format Files pdb .pdb, .ent, gzipped or not. Predictors write pLDDT into the B-factor column mmcif .cif, .mmcif, gzipped or not pae .pae.tsv (proteinfold) or .pae.json (AlphaFold DB, ColabFold)

The sample id the scan derives must equal the entity value of the residue tables, which is how a tile finds the structure of the protein it shows.

docs.title: Template Projects
docs.text:
Perfect for: nf-core pipelines and standardized bioinformatics workflows

Use when: You have output from a supported pipeline (e.g. nf-core/ampliseq) and want a fully configured project + dashboards in one command — without writing any YAML.

Templates are pre-packaged project configurations that ship with Depictio. Each template bundles a project YAML (with {DATA_ROOT} placeholders), bundled dashboards, and referenced data transformation recipes for a specific pipeline version.

docs.title: One-command setup
docs.text:
depictio ingest /data/my_ampliseq_run \
  --template nf-core/ampliseq/2.16.0

That single command:

  1. Resolves all {DATA_ROOT} placeholders, and the template's other variables, throughout the config
  2. Creates the project in MongoDB
  3. Discovers and processes all data collections (running recipes automatically)
  4. Imports the bundled dashboard

Without --template, the template is detected from the results directory when it can be, and since v1.16.0 a local directory no bundled template fits gets one composed from the catalog. Running the same command again with --update-config refreshes the project and keeps its dashboards as edited in the viewer; see Refreshing a project.

The results directory can also be an s3:// prefix, a manifest-driven template takes --manifest <url or path> in place of the directory, and any template can be pointed at other locations, collection by collection, with --bind TAG=LOCATION. The web UI creates a project from a run folder too, with From a run folder. See Remote data and manifests.

docs.title: When to use templates
docs.text:
Use templates when:

  • ✅ You ran a supported nf-core pipeline (e.g. ampliseq) and want instant visualization
  • ✅ You want a reproducible, versioned project setup you can share with collaborators
  • ✅ You prefer not to write project YAML from scratch

Use a manual YAML config when:

  • ✅ Your pipeline is not yet covered by a bundled template
  • ✅ You need highly customized data collection patterns or scan configurations
  • ✅ You want fine-grained control over which files are included

docs.title: Project Types Comparison
docs.text:
Choose the right project type for your workflow:

Feature Basic Projects Advanced Projects Template Projects Setup Complexity Minimal - Web UI or CLI CLI and YAML config; data collections can be added in the Web UI (v1.18.0+) Single CLI command, no YAML needed (WebUI planned) Data Sources UI File upload or CLI-based processing CLI-based processing CLI-based (pipeline output) File Organization Simple file management Structured directory patterns Fixed structure per template Multi-sample Support Single datasets Multi samples support Full support (template-specific) Data Processing Direct conversion Aggregation & cross-DC links Recipes + cross-DC links (pre-configured) Learning Curve Immediate Moderate (YAML knowledge) Minimal (just point at data dir) Scalability Small-medium datasets Large-scale studies Pipeline-scale (template-specific)

docs.title: How to Choose the Right Project Type
docs.text:
Choose Basic when:

  • ✅ You have a limited number of files ready for analysis
  • ✅ One-time analysis or ad-hoc exploration
  • ✅ Manual data preparation is acceptable
  • ✅ Quick insights are the primary goal

Choose Advanced when:

  • ✅ Automated pipelines generate your data
  • ✅ Standardized file organization exists
  • ✅ You need to aggregate data across samples/runs
  • ✅ Regular data updates are expected

Choose a Template when:

  • ✅ You ran a supported nf-core pipeline (e.g. ampliseq)
  • ✅ You want instant project + dashboards without writing YAML
  • ✅ Reproducibility and template provenance tracking matter

docs.title: Project Permissions
docs.text: Depictio implements a comprehensive role-based permission system:

docs.title: Permission Roles
docs.text:
Role Capabilities Owner Full control - edit, delete, manage permissions Editor Modify project data, create/edit dashboards Viewer Read-only access to project and dashboards

Since v1.18.0 a role can be given to a person or to a whole group, from the Groups section of the project's Permissions page. A person's role is the highest of their own and their groups': a direct viewer whose group owns the project is an owner. Writing a data collection needs editor, deleting one owner. The project settings no longer change who has access: sharing goes through Permissions only.

docs.title: Everyone with access (v1.19.0+)
docs.text: The Permissions page sums direct and group grants into Everyone with access: one row per person, highest role first, with every grant behind it. Typing a group's name in the add box previews its members before Add group, flagging those who already have access. Both show members' emails, so only those who may change the sharing see them: owners, system admins and the admins of an owning group.

docs.title: Public Projects
docs.text:
Projects can be made public by:

  • Setting is_public: true in configuration
  • Using the web interface toggle

Public projects are:

  • ✅ Visible to all users
  • ✅ Read-only for non-members
  • ✅ Searchable in project listings
  • ❌ Only editable by owners and editors
  • ❌ Not editable by viewers or anonymous users

docs.title: Project deletion
docs.text:
Deleting a project (via the Web UI or DELETE /depictio/api/v1/projects/{id}) cascades to all dependent state:

  • Workflows declared in the project
  • Data collections (and their MongoDB documents)
  • Dashboards owned by the project
  • S3 objects under s3://<bucket>/{project_id}/

There is no soft-delete or trash bin — once the operation completes, the project's data is unrecoverable. Use Project migrate to take a portable backup ZIP before deletion if you need rollback capability.

Self-migration shortcut

Migrating a project to the same instance (source == target) skips the S3 copy step but still produces a complete export ZIP — useful for backing up immediately before a delete.

docs.title: Delta Lake Backend
docs.text:
All project data is automatically converted to Delta Lake format which provides following benefits:

  • ACID Transactions - Reliable data consistency
  • Time Travel - Version history and rollback capabilities
  • Schema Evolution - Handle changing data structures
  • Optimized Queries - Fast dashboard performance
  • Compression - Efficient storage utilization

Future Depictio versions will support aforementioned features progressively, enhancing user experience and data management capabilities.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
Recipes are the data transformation layer of the Depictio CLI. They convert raw bioinformatics pipeline output files into clean, dashboard-ready Polars DataFrames — automatically, reproducibly, and with full validation.

Upstream — Workflow Bioinformatics pipeline nf-core / Nextflow / Snakemake ↓ Raw output files
  • wide CSV
  • nested TSV
  • non-standard headers
↓ Recipe
  • reformat & reshape
  • wide → long
  • rename columns
  • compute metrics
↓ Downstream — Depictio Tidy DataFrame
  • long format
  • clean schema
  • validated types
↓ Dashboard figures & tables

docs.title: What is a Recipe?
docs.text:
In one sentence: a recipe is the reshaping step a template runs for you to turn a raw pipeline output into a tidy, dashboard-ready table. Templates bundle their recipes — you rarely write one unless you're adding support for a new pipeline output.

A recipe is a plain Python module that describes how to transform one or more raw files into a single tidy DataFrame. Each recipe lives in depictio/projects/<pipeline>/recipes/ and declares:

  • SOURCES: input files to read (paths relative to --data-dir, or references to other data collections via dc_ref), each with the input_schema it reads: the columns the file must contain
  • OUTPUT_SCHEMA: required output columns and their Polars data types
  • OPTIONAL_OUTPUT_SCHEMA (optional): columns that may or may not be present (e.g. user-defined metadata columns)
  • transform(sources): a pure function that takes loaded DataFrames and returns the output DataFrame

A # INPUT SCHEMA: comment line sits above SOURCES and a # OUTPUT SCHEMA: line above OUTPUT_SCHEMA, so a recipe reads as a contract from the top of the file.

Recipes are used in two ways:

  1. Standalone testing: depictio dev recipe run executes a recipe locally against a data directory, so you can validate your data before registering a project.
  2. Project integration: a data_collection with source: "transformed" tells the CLI to run the recipe during depictio ingest, storing the result as a Delta Lake table.

docs.title: The 5-Checkpoint Validation Pipeline (v1.12.0+)
docs.text:
Every recipe execution, whether via depictio dev recipe run or depictio ingest, runs through five automatic checkpoints:

# Checkpoint What it checks 1 Load Import the recipe module; verify SOURCES, OUTPUT_SCHEMA, and a callable transform() exist 2 Resolve Find each file under --data-dir; skip optional sources gracefully; fail fast if required files are missing 3 Input schema Assert every column in each source's input_schema is present in the file that was read, with a compatible dtype 4 Transform Call transform(sources), verify it returns a non-empty pl.DataFrame 5 Output schema Assert every column in OUTPUT_SCHEMA is present with the correct dtype; validate OPTIONAL_OUTPUT_SCHEMA columns if present

Before v1.12.0 a recipe ran four checkpoints: there was no input-schema check (3), and the output schema was named EXPECTED_SCHEMA.

If any checkpoint fails, execution stops with a clear error message pointing to the exact problem.

The input check is deliberately loose on types: readers infer them from the data, so a text or all-null column passes wherever the recipe casts the value itself, and one numeric type stands for another. A missing column always fails, naming the source and the column:

RecipeError: Recipe arriba/fusions.py: source 'fusions' lacks input column(s) ['#gene1']. Got columns: ['gene1', ...]

Options:
